One thing that I have been a little bit excited about recently is a new tool I'm calling [stringency](https://github.com/santangelo-lab/stringency). This is basically a belay device and top rope safety harness system for scientists using AI to automate their data analysis. I'm building it to help my lab members run the correct bioinformatic analysis on new data, where *correct* implies that whatever the AI does is grounded in sound, commonly accepted analysis techniques and completely reproducible/traceable.

![](../../assets/software/stringency-belay.png){fig-alt="Illustration of a belayer holding the rope for an AI agent climbing a data-analysis wall" width="60%" fig-align="center"}

## Biologists are the right people for this

The fact is with today's leading AI models you can do most any bioinformatic work without knowing a single thing about writing code. This is not a bad thing! Biologists thinking deeply about their scientific questions and collecting data are probably the best suited to be using AI in this way. They have the deep domain knowledge that any generalist model will inevitably lack, and they can use it to cut through the professional-sounding noise that a model often produces when given an unfocused task or question. Scientists are trained to ask strong, focused, and verifiable questions. Coincidentally, this is exactly what an AI needs to be given in order to help produce helpful results in data analysis. What's more, scientists know their data best. Giving them the tools to successfully analyze a dataset from start to finish avoids the dilution or "thrown over the wall" problem that plagues current collaborations or outsourcing of this work to a separate team member or worse...a core service group.

## But AI alone is a poor fit for science

However, AI models with their stochastic, overly-confident nature and their transient lifespan can be unpredictable and are by definition not reproducible, none of which is a good fit for scientific work. For example: perhaps an AI agent might approach a problem in an unusual or unconventional way when faced with an initial roadblock. Or maybe an agent successfully processes some data, but then the session ends and all provenance of how the outputs were generated is lost with the model's death. Or worse, what if the agent asserts something about your data driven entirely by a hallucination, and builds off of that for the next few hours. You look at the spreadsheet it generated at the end and the numbers are completely wrong, or maybe you can't even tell. At this point there is no way to answer the question: *how did you do this?* And without the knowledge of an experienced analyst it's also very hard to answer the question *why did you do it this way?*

Scientists need a way to leverage the automation, the strong logical thinking and the significant programming ability AI brings to the table. But it needs to be in a way that is guided and constrained so that even those with no coding or technical knowledge of the underlying analysis work can drive the work forward in a responsible way.

**Enter stringency.**
